notes.meaning: God told Moses to make the tabernacle's inner dwelling with ten curtains of fine twisted linen. These curtains were decorated with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with cherubim skillfully worked into the cloth. Cherubim are winged heavenly creatures who attend God's throne. Because this beautiful layer hung on the inside, it showed God's kingly glory to the priests serving within.

Each curtain was forty-two feet long and six feet wide, so every piece was the exact same size. Five of these curtains were sewn together into one wide sheet, and the remaining five were sewn together into a second matching sheet. Making two large sections instead of one giant piece made the tabernacle covering easier to take down and carry.

Fifty blue loops were placed along the edge of each large curtain sheet so the two halves lined up evenly. Fifty gold clasps then fastened the loops together, linking both halves into one continuous ceiling and wall covering. In this way, the individual pieces became a single, unified sacred home for God.

God ordered a second layer of eleven curtains woven from coarse goats' hair to be placed over the tabernacle. Each curtain was forty-five feet long and six feet wide, making them three feet longer than the inner linen curtains. The dark, thick goats' hair provided a tough covering like the tents of desert travelers, shielding the sacred sanctuary.

The eleven goats' hair curtains were joined into two sections, one with five panels and the other with six. The extra sixth curtain was doubled over at the front to form a neat border above the doorway. Fifty loops along the edges were connected with fifty bronze clasps, firmly joining the outer tent into one unit.

Because the goats' hair tent was larger than the linen curtains beneath it, extra cloth was left over. Half of the extra curtain hung down over the back of the tabernacle, and an extra foot and a half hung over each side. This ensured that the delicate linen layer underneath was completely protected from the sun, rain, and desert sand.

Two more protective coverings were made to go over the goats' hair tent. One layer was made of ram skins dyed red, and on top of that went a layer of strong, weather-resistant fine leather. These tough outer skins shielded the holy dwelling from fierce weather and desert dust.

Upright wall frames were built from sturdy acacia wood to support the tabernacle's coverings. Each wooden frame stood fifteen feet high and over two feet wide, with two wooden pegs carved at the bottom. These pegs fit into bases on the ground so the frames would stand firmly in place.

Twenty upright frames were constructed to form the south wall of the tabernacle. Underneath them rested forty heavy silver bases, providing two solid foundations for the two pegs of each frame. These silver bases kept the walls steady and raised them cleanly above the desert ground.

The north wall was built in the same way, using twenty acacia wood frames. Forty silver bases were placed beneath them, with two bases supporting each upright frame. This gave both sides of the sanctuary equal strength and balance.

Six wooden frames were made for the rear wall facing west, behind the Most Holy Place. Two special frames were also crafted for the back corners of the building. These corner pieces helped tie the rear wall and side walls together into a firm structure.

The corner frames were joined together from bottom to top and locked at the peak with a single ring. This brought the back wall to a total of eight frames standing on sixteen silver bases, two under each frame. These solid corners prevented the walls from shifting in desert winds.

Five crossbars made of acacia wood were prepared for the south wall, five for the north, and five for the west rear wall. These bars slid through rings on the frames to hold the upright boards tightly together. The middle bar ran along the center of the wall from one end to the other, locking the whole side securely.

The wooden frames and the crossbars were overlaid with gleaming gold. Rings of solid gold were also fastened to the frames to hold the crossbars in place. This made the inside of the tabernacle shine with royal beauty for the Lord.

God commanded Moses to set up the tabernacle according to the exact plan shown to him on Mount Sinai. Every part of the design had spiritual meaning and purpose, leaving no room for human invention. God's people are reminded that true worship must always follow what God Himself has revealed.

A thick inner veil was woven from fine linen with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, decorated with figures of cherubim. It hung by gold hooks from four acacia posts overlaid with gold, which rested on four silver bases. This ornate curtain served as a screen to close off the innermost room of the sanctuary.

The veil was hung beneath the ceiling clasps, and the ark of the Testimony was placed right behind it. This curtain created a clear divide between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place, where God's presence dwelt. Under this old covenant, the curtain kept people back, showing that full access to God was not yet open to everyone.

The mercy seat was placed on top of the ark of the Testimony inside the Most Holy Place. Outside the veil in the Holy Place, the table for the showbread was set on the north side, and the golden lampstand stood across from it on the south side. These holy items provided constant food and light before God in His earthly dwelling.

For the entrance to the tent on the east side, an embroidered curtain was made of fine linen and blue, purple, and scarlet yarn. It hung on gold hooks from five gold-covered acacia posts set into five bronze bases. This entrance screen kept the holy interior private while welcoming the priests in to serve the Lord.
